text: A fasting or non-fasting lipid panel should be repeated 4 to 12 weeks after starting or changing statin therapy to assess adherence and response.

Smoking cessation is the single most effective intervention to slow the progression of COPD; every smoker should be offered counselling plus pharmacotherapy such as varenicline or nicotine replacement.
Lifestyle measures for hypertension include dietary sodium below 2 grams per day, the DASH diet, at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week, weight loss and limiting alcohol.

Moderate-intensity statin therapy is recommended for people with diabetes aged 40 to 75 years without established cardiovascular disease; high-intensity statin is recommended if additional risk factors are present.
Adults with type 2 diabetes should have a dilated retinal examination at diagnosis and at least every 1 to 2 years thereafter to screen for diabetic retinopathy.

Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium above 6.0 mmol/L or any level with ECG changes) requires intravenous calcium gluconate for membrane stabilisation, followed by insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells.
Loop diuretics such as furosemide are used to relieve congestion in heart failure and should be adjusted to the lowest dose that maintains euvolaemia; they do not improve survival.
First-line pharmacotherapy for most adults with type 2 diabetes is metformin, started alongside lifestyle modification, unless it is contraindicated or not tolerated.
Guideline-directed therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has four pillars: an ARNI or ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor.

First-line antihypertensive drug classes are thiazide-type diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and calcium channel blockers; beta-blockers are not first-line unless there is a compelling indication.
Chronic kidney disease is staged by eGFR: G1 90 or above, G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29 and G5 below 15 mL/min/1.73 m2, together with the albuminuria category.
Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and should not be initiated when eGFR is between 30 and 45; the dose should be reviewed at eGFR below 45.
An ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker should not be combined because the combination increases hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury without added benefit.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed when HbA1c is 6.5% or higher, fasting plasma glucose is 126 mg/dL or higher, or a 2-hour glucose is 200 mg/dL or higher on an oral glucose tolerance test, confirmed by repeat testing.
COPD is confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry showing an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 in a patient with symptoms and a history of exposure such as tobacco smoke.
All adults with diabetes should receive an annual influenza vaccine, and pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for adults aged 65 years and older and for younger adults with chronic conditions.
Mild hypoglycaemia (glucose below 70 mg/dL) in a conscious patient is treated with 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, rechecking glucose after 15 minutes and repeating if still below 70 mg/dL.

The apixaban dose for atrial fibrillation is reduced from 5 mg to 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two of the following are present: age 80 or older, weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or higher.
For adults with mild asthma, as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol is the preferred reliever; short-acting beta-agonist alone is no longer recommended.

Obesity is defined as a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher; pharmacotherapy may be considered at BMI 30 or above, or 27 or above with a weight-related comorbidity, in addition to lifestyle intervention.

An ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker is recommended for patients with chronic kidney disease and albuminuria (urine albumin-creatinine ratio 30 mg/g or higher), titrated to the highest tolerated dose.
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be avoided in patients with chronic kidney disease stage G3 or worse because they can precipitate acute kidney injury and worsen hypertension.

Adults with suspected infection should be screened for sepsis; a qSOFA score of 2 or more (altered mentation, systolic blood pressure 100 mmHg or below, respiratory rate 22 or above) indicates high risk of poor outcome.
A spacer device should be used with pressurised metered-dose inhalers to improve lung deposition and reduce oropharyngeal side effects, especially in children and during exacerbations.
For people with type 2 diabetes who have chronic kidney disease or heart failure, an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended independent of HbA1c to reduce kidney and cardiovascular events.
Levothyroxine replacement for overt hypothyroidism is typically started at 1.6 micrograms per kilogram per day, with TSH rechecked 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change.
The blood pressure target for most adults with diabetes is below 130/80 mmHg if it can be achieved safely.
Urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol is started at 100 mg daily and titrated every 2 to 4 weeks to a serum urate target below 6 mg/dL; a lower starting dose is used in chronic kidney disease.
A serum ferritin below 30 ng/mL indicates iron deficiency; in the presence of inflammation, ferritin below 100 ng/mL with transferrin saturation below 20% also suggests iron deficiency.

Asthma treatment should be stepped up if a patient needs reliever medication more than twice a week, wakes at night because of asthma, or has had an exacerbation requiring oral steroids in the past year.
Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban are preferred over warfarin for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation because of similar efficacy and less intracranial bleeding.
A reasonable HbA1c target for most non-pregnant adults with diabetes is below 7%; a less stringent target such as below 8% is appropriate for frail older adults or those with limited life expectancy.
In patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, the LDL cholesterol goal is below 70 mg/dL, using a high-intensity statin and adding ezetimibe if the goal is not reached.
For rate control in atrial fibrillation, a beta-blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is first-line, aiming for a resting heart rate below 110 beats per minute.

Patients reporting statin-associated muscle symptoms should have creatine kinase measured; if symptoms are intolerable, the statin can be paused and rechallenged at a lower dose or with an alternative statin.
A comprehensive foot examination, including inspection, pulses and loss-of-protective-sensation testing, should be performed at least annually in every person with diabetes.
Hypertension is diagnosed when the average of readings on two or more occasions is 130/80 mmHg or higher; out-of-office measurement is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.
Initial maintenance therapy for symptomatic COPD with a history of exacerbations is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, with a long-acting beta-agonist added if symptoms persist.
Oral anticoagulation is recommended for atrial fibrillation when the CHA2DS2-VASc score is 2 or higher in men or 3 or higher in women.
ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated in pregnancy; preferred agents for hypertension in pregnancy are labetalol, nifedipine and methyldopa.
